note: The first write path this close to the trust root: a human ratifies a machine-proposed decision-graph edge from the Triage tab by signing it in the browser. Built by a sub-agent in an isolated worktree, then audited hardest of the session and run through the security-review skill. The crux — that the browser signs the exact bytes the server verifies — was proven, not asserted: the actual JS pyJsonArray(['edge',src,dst,kind]) was run in Node against signing._edge_message across three cases including quote-escaping and non-ASCII, byte-identical each time. Security review found no bypass: signing.py and ledger.py untouched, verify-before-write reused verbatim, read-only enforced at the dispatch layer, the refusal error leaks no key, the new confirm dialog renders decision text via text nodes not innerHTML, CSRF inherited. One non-blocking hardening follow-up was surfaced (below), not a blocker.

decisions.question: How does a human ratify a machine-proposed decision-graph edge from the browser, and what must the server trust to accept it?
decisions.commitment: POST /api/edge/seal accepts a client-produced Ed25519 signature over the frozen 4-element message ['edge', src_id, dst_id, kind] and forwards it to DecisionMemory.seal_edge unchanged -- the endpoint itself never signs. The verifier is resolved by the same rule as a client-signed decision seal (_verifier_for_seal, generalized only by which payload field carries the signature): a signed-in session names the verifier when no signature is offered, and a payload-named verifier is trusted only on the strength of a signature that verifies for that exact name, checked downstream in seal_edge. kind is validated against the closed EDGE_KINDS set (a bad kind is a 400, distinct from the 403 a refused signature gets). Confirm only: rejecting a proposed edge is out of scope (no schema today) and is the next bite.
decisions.why: It mirrors the existing decision-seal ceremony (/api/seal) exactly rather than inventing a second identity-resolution rule that could drift from the first. The covenant is mechanical here: signing.edge_is_valid returns False for an empty signature, always, and constraints_on traverses an edge only when it returns True -- so a machine-proposed edge cannot constrain anything until a human signs it, and the machine has no path to produce that signature (the browser's private key is non-extractable; seal_edge only verifies). Byte-equality between the browser signer and the server verifier was proven end-to-end, because a mismatch would either silently reject every real confirmation or, worse, let a human sign bytes other than what is checked.
decisions.doors_closed: No server-side signing path for edges (unlike decision seals, which can auto-sign under a shared HMAC key) -- an edge can only ever be ratified by a signature produced outside this process. No second verify or second write built beside seal_edge. /api/triage and /api/graph stay read-only, GET-only, with no persisted-edge coupling to Triage's in-memory proposed-edge computation (so a confirmed edge is authoritative in the Graph tab and the ledger; the Triage tab remembers a confirmation session-locally rather than mutating the read-only recompute). Follow-up, filed not fixed: seal_edge does not verify that src_id/dst_id exist or share a domain the way propose_edge does -- a valid key-holder could seal a junk edge between unknown ids; unreachable via the shipped UI (ids come from real /api/triage decisions), low severity, worth a small consistency fix in decision.py.
